name: Flashbulb Memory
statement: A shocking, consequential event can imprint a vivid, confidently held memory of the moment one learned of it, though not necessarily an accurate one.
meaning: A flashbulb memory is an unusually vivid, detailed, and long-lasting memory not of a shocking public event itself but of the personal circumstances in which one first learned of it. Brown and Kulik described such memories as capturing details like place, ongoing activity, the informant, and one's own emotional reaction. People hold them with exceptional confidence.
mechanism: Brown and Kulik proposed a "special mechanism": when an event exceeds thresholds of surprise and consequentiality, an emotional-arousal system lays down a near-permanent, photographic-feeling record of the surrounding details. Later research instead emphasizes that heightened emotion and frequent rehearsal boost vividness and confidence more than they boost objective accuracy.

examples.text: Brown and Kulik's original work drew on people's detailed recollections of where they were when they heard President Kennedy had been shot.
Studies of the 1986 Space Shuttle Challenger explosion found memories drifted substantially over time, with a minority retaining detailed accurate accounts months later despite high confidence.
Long-term studies of 9/11 recollections showed people stayed highly confident even as the consistency of their reported details declined.

whyItMatters: Flashbulb memories reveal a striking dissociation between subjective confidence and objective accuracy, a caution for eyewitness testimony and personal-history claims. They are a key case study in how emotion and rehearsal shape autobiographical memory.
limits: Evidence largely undercuts the "special mechanism" claim: these memories decay and distort like ordinary memories, and their hallmark is perceived accuracy, not real accuracy. One study found under 35% had detailed Challenger memories eight months later, yet confidence remained high even as content shifted.
misreadings: A flashbulb memory is not a reliable "photograph" of events; its vividness and confidence do not guarantee that its details are correct.
origin: Roger Brown and James Kulik coined the term in 1977.

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Flashbulb memory" article — supports the 1977 Brown & Kulik coinage, the characteristic features, and the finding that these memories are special in perceived rather than actual accuracy.
Simply Psychology's "Flashbulb Memory" — supports the definition as exceptionally clear memories of emotionally significant events and the 1977 coinage.
